one_liner: Pure-Mojo regex library with a re-like API and hybrid DFA/lazy-DFA/NFA engines; first-party micro-benchmarks claim wins over CPython re and Rust regex.
what_it_does: A Mojo package (`pixi add mojo-regex`) with Python-re-style free functions: match_first (re.match), search, findall, sub (with \1 group interpolation) and split. compile_regex returns a CompiledRegex with match_first, match_next, match_all, is_match and sub, and the experimental regex.comptime_regex API (`search["hello"](text)`) builds the DFA at compile time. It works on UTF-8 StringSlices and returns Match objects whose lifetime is tied to the input text. Its syntax is a subset of re's: named groups, case-insensitive matching, non-greedy quantifiers, \b, Unicode classes, multiline and dot-all modes, lookaround, and \S, \D and \W are all missing.
how_it_is_fast: HybridMatcher classifies each pattern at compile time and routes it to one engine. Simple patterns go to a DFA with SIMD character-class matchers (nibble lookup tables, vectorised range checks) and a two-byte memchr-style literal scan. Large or nested alternations go to a lazy DFA built from a PikeVM program, with a SIMD first-byte prefilter. $-anchored patterns use a OnePass NFA, and everything else uses a backtracking NFA with two-way literal prefiltering. Leading or trailing `.*` gets an rfind or two-way shortcut, guarded by a no-newline check. findall on patterns with a rare required byte (the `@` in an email, the `-` in a phone number) memchr-scans for that byte and backs up to a candidate start. Compiled patterns are cached in a process-global dict keyed by pattern hash, and the comptime API removes that hash and probe as well (about 17 ns per call, CHANGELOG).
when_to_use: Mojo code that needs regular expressions and whose patterns fit the supported subset: ASCII classes, \d, \w, \s, bounded quantifiers, alternation, groups and anchors.

Extraction and validation loops over ASCII text, such as phone numbers, dates, serial IDs and emails. On the matched-input rows, findall was about 5-60x faster than CPython re and about 1.1-8x faster than Rust regex.
Short inputs where per-call overhead dominates, such as validating single fields. The comptime API measured 36 vs 53 ns per call against the runtime API on a short literal search.
Porting Python re code to Mojo, since the function names and sub() group syntax are close to re's.
when_not_to_use: Patterns that need case-insensitivity, non-greedy quantifiers, \b, lookaround, named groups, Unicode classes, multiline or dot-all modes, or the negated shorthands \S, \D and \W.
Untrusted patterns or inputs: complex patterns fall back to a backtracking NFA, and ReDoS protection is still an open issue (#31).
Multi-threaded programs: the compiled-regex cache and the one-slot sub() cache are process-global with no locking, and the source warns that concurrent sub() calls can apply the wrong template.

Production code that needs stability. The project is a 0.x release with several wrong-match bugs fixed in 2026 (#114, #120, #39 state corruption, DFA parser bugs that 'silently returned zero matches' before v0.8.0), an open double-free at process exit (#97) and constant churn from Mojo toolchain upgrades.

Throughput-critical use of the current release. CHANGELOG v0.20.0 reports the Mojo 1.0 build as about 13% slower by geomean than v0.13.0, the version behind the published table, and advises staying on v0.13.0 / Mojo 0.26.x for performance.

integration.form: module (Mojo package installed with pixi from the conda channel)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the Mojo standard library (pyyaml only for the optional mojopkg build feature)
integration.min_toolchain: Mojo ==1.0.0 exactly (pinned in pixi.toml for v0.21.0). The published benchmarks used v0.13.0 on Mojo 0.26.2.
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe. The global pattern cache and the sub() identity cache are process-global with no locking (matcher.mojo comment: 'concurrent sub() calls from different threads can race and produce a torn state').
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the function names follow Python re (match_first for re.match, search, findall, sub, split), but it is a Mojo API with a smaller syntax, no flags and ASCII-only classes, and it does not replace re inside Python

gotchas: Harness flaw in the Rust column (new finding): in 13 of the 71 Mojo-vs-Rust rows, benchmarks/rust/src/bench_engine.rs and lib.rs time a different input, pattern or operation from the Mojo harness. (1) literal_match_short and literal_match_long put 'hello' 10x deeper in Rust's text (offsets 10,001 and 100,001 vs 1,000 and 10,000), so Rust scans 10x more bytes; per byte, Rust is about 2.5x and 1.4x faster (derived), not 4.1x and 7.3x slower. (2) range_lowercase, range_digits and predefined_digits run on Rust's 'abc123XYZ' text, where the match is 3 bytes at offset 0 or 3, against Mojo's 10,000-letter text, so Rust's 3.1-3.8x 'wins' are artifacts too. (3) group_alternation times (a|b)* in Rust vs (a|b) in Mojo, match_all_simple times 'a' on alphabet text vs 'hello' on medium_text, and literal_prefix_short times hello.*world vs hello.*. (4) literal_prefix_long, required_literal_short, no_literal_baseline and alternation_common_prefix give Rust texts 10-50x shorter (SHORT_TEXT x10 vs x100, x100 vs x1000, EMAIL_TEXT x1 vs x50), and the last two time find_iter().collect() against Mojo's single anchored match_first. (5) wildcard_match_any is the '.*' shortcut below. On the 58 rows whose inputs and operations match, the Mojo-vs-Rust geomean is about 2.77x (Mojo faster on 49, Rust on 8; derived from page data), not 3.47x.

Correctness bug behind the wildcard_match_any row: HybridMatcher special-cases a pattern that is exactly '.*' (matcher.mojo _is_wildcard_match_any). match_first, match_next and match_all then return one Match covering the rest of the text without running a regex or checking for newlines, and is_match returns true. On text containing '\n', results therefore differ from re, where '.' stops at a newline. The bench text has no newline, so the 5,454x (Python) and 45,718x (Rust) ratios time a constant return. The leading and trailing '.*' fast paths in nfa.mojo do check text.find("\n") == -1.

Python-column caveats: the five is_match rows time Mojo's short-circuit bool against bool(re.match(...)), which runs the full greedy match over about 10,000 characters (7,434-18,013x). Python's nanosecond rows sit on a CPython call-overhead floor of roughly 120-160 ns (alternation_simple 123.9 ns, anchor_start 129.9 ns). Mojo samples are at least 10 ms against 1 ms for Python and Rust, and the Mojo harness has no black_box. Without the is_match and wildcard rows, the geomean vs re is about 14.7x over 70 rows (derived).

Stale and noisy numbers: comparison.md was last refreshed on 2026-05-01 for v0.13.0 on Mojo 0.26.2 and names no CPU. The v0.13.0 changelog says that run's Rust numbers came from 'a fresher Rust toolchain (~1.5x faster than the v0.12.0 measurement)', so the baseline moved between runs. The README's 'beats Rust on 61%' does not match comparison.md (59 of 71 rows, 83%).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Use mojo-regex only from Mojo code whose patterns fit its subset. Elsewhere, the Rust regex sibling is the engine it is measured against: on rows with matched inputs it trails mojo-regex by about 2.8x geomean on these micro-benchmarks, but it is faster per byte on the long literal-scan rows and has the full syntax. Ferroni is the choice when Oniguruma syntax compatibility matters.
verified_claims_summary: The claim comes from the first-party comparison.md: mojo-regex 0.13.0 on Mojo 0.26.2 (default optimisation) against CPython 3.12 re and Rust regex 1.10 (opt-level 3, LTO, codegen-units 1, target-cpu=native), with pre-compiled patterns and median timing over 500 ms, on an unnamed CPU. It reports geomeans of 24.54x vs re over 76 rows and 3.47x vs Rust over 71 rows. Dropping rows where the harnesses do different work leaves about 14.7x vs re (70 rows) and about 2.8x vs Rust (58 rows), both derived from page data.
status_note: Active single-maintainer 0.x project (v0.21.0, last commit 2026-09-01, MIT, 18 stars) that tracks Mojo releases closely. It is copyable, but it is pinned to Mojo ==1.0.0, ships only for linux-64 and osx-arm64, and its own changelog says the current Mojo 1.0 build is about 13% slower than the build behind the published numbers.
